common_name: Ruth Holleyman Louisiana Iris (Classic Deep Wine-Red Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall so roots establish before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay damp.

directions: Ruth Holleyman is a long-admired Louisiana iris cultivar valued for flowers in an unusually deep wine-red to burgundy self tone, ruffled and heavy in substance, that rank among the darkest reds achieved in this hybrid group. Blooms open in mid-spring on sturdy stalks held above strap-like foliage, and the rich color holds well even in bright sun rather than fading to pink. Like other Louisiana iris, it performs best where soil stays consistently damp, making it a strong candidate for a bog garden, pond edge, or naturally soggy low spot. Divide crowded clumps every few years in late summer, replanting divisions promptly since Louisiana iris rhizomes decline quickly if left to dry out.

common_name: Contraband Girl Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Rose-Pink Award Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil; give this ruffled pink cultivar full sun to keep its color saturated and to encourage the heaviest bloom.

directions: Contraband Girl carries heavily ruffled, rosy orchid-pink flowers with a gold-touched signal patch at the throat, a color and form that made it a standout among pink-toned Louisiana iris introductions and earned it lasting popularity with Gulf South growers. Its name nods to the historic Barataria-area bayou country associated with early privateers and smugglers, a fitting regional touch for a hybrid bred from bayou-native species. It flowers in mid- to late spring above clumping, sword-like foliage and multiplies steadily in reliably wet ground. Plant it at a pond margin or rain garden low point and divide congested fans every three to four years in late summer for best vigor.

common_name: Bout De Zan Louisiana Iris (Near-Black Deep Red-Purple Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall for establishment before spring bloom; the darkest Louisiana iris colors like this one hold their depth best with steady moisture and at least a half day of direct sun.

directions: Bout De Zan takes its playful Cajun-French name (roughly, a mischievous little scamp) and pairs it with flowers in an exceptionally deep, near-black red-purple, among the darkest tones bred into the Louisiana iris class. The velvety falls and standards show only a thin flash of a darker signal line, keeping the overall effect almost solid and dramatic against paler companion cultivars. Bloom comes in mid-spring on well-branched stalks above typical strap-shaped Louisiana iris foliage. Because dark pigments can look muddy in deep shade, give it full sun and steadily moist to wet soil so the color reads as rich black-red rather than dull brown.

common_name: Sinfonietta Louisiana Iris (Pastel Peach-Apricot Blend Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall in consistently moist, slightly acidic soil; light partial shade in hot climates can help hold this pastel blend's coloring longer than in baking full sun.

directions: Sinfonietta brings a softer palette to the Louisiana iris border, opening ruffled blooms in a warm peach-to-apricot blend that shades toward pale pink at the petal edges, a departure from the saturated reds, blues, and purples more typical of this hybrid group. The gentle color combination pairs easily with both the darkest cultivars and the whites in a mixed bed, softening high-contrast plantings. Flowers appear in mid-spring on upright stems above the clumping, grass-like foliage typical of the class. Keep soil consistently damp through bloom and into summer, and divide crowded clumps in late summer every three to four years to keep flower size and color quality from declining.

common_name: Wood Violet Louisiana Iris (Deep Blue-Violet Award Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun for the deepest violet color and heaviest bloom.

directions: Wood Violet produces richly saturated blue-violet flowers with a small gold-brushed signal at the base of each fall, a color combination that has kept it a favorite among growers seeking a true deep-violet Louisiana iris rather than the more common softer blues. Its ruffled form and heavy substance let the flowers hold up well through spring rain, an important trait for a plant so often grown at pond edges and in rain gardens. Clumps bulk up steadily in reliably wet, fertile ground and bloom in mid-spring on stems well above the sword-shaped leaves. Divide every three to four years in late summer, discarding any soft or rotted rhizome sections before replanting.

common_name: C'est Si Bon Louisiana Iris (Pastel Lavender-Cream Blend Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall in consistently moist, slightly acidic soil; this pastel-blend cultivar appreciates a little afternoon shade in the hottest Gulf Coast gardens to prevent bleaching.

directions: C'est Si Bon takes its French Louisiana name from a cheerful phrase meaning roughly "it's so good," and its flowers live up to it with a soft blend of lavender and cream that shifts subtly across each ruffled petal. The gentle two-tone effect gives it a lighter, more delicate presence in the border than the bold self-colored cultivars often associated with this group. Bloom occurs in mid-spring on branched stems rising above typical clumping, strap-like Louisiana iris foliage. It shares the group's need for steady moisture and benefits from division of crowded fans every three to four years in late summer to keep bloom quality strong.

common_name: Michele Bourque Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Rose-Pink Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall for establishment before spring bloom; consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and full sun bring out the deepest rose-pink coloring.

directions: Michele Bourque bears heavily ruffled flowers in a clear, saturated rose-pink self, a Cajun-family surname cultivar name that reflects the strong ties between Louisiana iris breeding and south Louisiana's bayou communities. The rounded, overlapping petals give the bloom a full, rose-like appearance rather than the narrower flare of older Louisiana iris forms. Flowering comes in mid-spring on sturdy stalks above the group's typical strappy foliage, and clumps expand readily where soil stays damp through the growing season. Divide every three to four years in late summer, replanting divisions right away to prevent the fleshy rhizomes from drying out.

common_name: Sun Fury Louisiana Iris (Warm Orange-Gold Blend Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in late summer to fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun, which intensifies this cultivar's warm gold-and-orange tones.

directions: Sun Fury glows with a fiery blend of orange, gold, and warm red tones that draws directly on the copper coloring contributed to Louisiana iris hybrids by native Iris fulva, making it one of the warmer-toned cultivars available in the class. The blended, sunset-like effect intensifies toward the petal edges, giving each ruffled bloom a lit-from-within quality in strong spring light. It flowers in mid-spring on upright stems above clumping, sword-shaped foliage and multiplies steadily in reliably wet ground. Give it full sun and steady moisture, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer to sustain strong color and bloom count.
